facts.claim: The digital single 'I'm Alive / Verbal Expressions' by Johnny Thunder was released 7 January 2011 by Parlophone Records. It has two tracks: 'I'm Alive' (2:56) and 'Verbal Expressions of T.V.' (2:47).
'I'm Alive' was written by Tommy James and Peter Lucia of Tommy James and the Shondells. Thunder's version is a cover.
The Qobuz listing for the 2011 release carries a 1969 phonographic copyright date for 'I'm Alive'. It credits Teddy Vann as producer of the B-side, 'Verbal Expressions of T.V.'
AllMusic's credits for the release list Tommy James and Peter Lucia as composers and Teddy Vann as producer.
The song was first issued as a 1969 single on the small New York label Calla Records, backed with 'Verbal Expressions of T.V.' It did not sell well enough to sustain his career.
Tommy James is credited as 'Arranger and Musical Concept' on the Calla single (C-161). The record has heavy fuzz guitar over a funky beat.
Songfacts says Thunder howls on this track, unlike his usual soft R&B vocal style on 'Loop De Loop'. It describes the vibe as closer to garage rock than to R&B or pop.
Thunder told Billboard author Wayne Jancik that 'I'm Alive' was his first true rock effort. He also cited Bob Dylan's Rolling Stone remark about it.
In a 1969 Rolling Stone interview with Jann Wenner, Bob Dylan said he heard 'I'm Alive' on the radio and called it one of the most powerful records he had ever heard.

Johnny Thunder was born Leroy 'Gilbert' Hamilton in Leesburg, Florida, on 15 August 1931 and died 6 September 2024. His biggest hit was 'Loop de Loop' (1963), produced by Teddy Vann, which reached no. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100. His labels included Diamond, Capitol, Vee Jay, Calla and Stateside.

research.lineage: A 1969 Calla Records cover of a Tommy James and the Shondells song, recorded by an early-'60s R&B and novelty-pop singer, it sits in the late-'60s fuzz-guitar garage, soul and funk-rock tradition.

draft:
"I'm no stone," Johnny Thunder sings, and the backing voices answer, "I'm alive." Then: "I'm no rock." Then, half-swallowed, "No piece of metal." It's a strange list to have to make. Nobody needs to announce they aren't made of metal unless someone has been treating them that way, and that's the pressure under all the joy of **I'm Alive**. The song is a shout of being here, and it's also a case being argued.

The song came from Tommy James and Peter Lucia of Tommy James and the Shondells, and James is credited with the arrangement and "musical concept" on Thunder's 1969 single for Calla, a small New York label. Thunder was six years past "Loop de Loop," the 1963 Teddy Vann production that went to No. 4. This was a different animal. Thunder later told the writer Wayne Jancik it was his first true rock record, and you can hear him leaning into the change. The voice is clear but carries a raw edge, pushed forward and full of energy. The band drives at a medium-fast clip: a snare that snaps, a bass walking underneath, an electric guitar chopping rhythm chords, and a keyboard holding long chords that keep the whole thing warm. Backing singers double and harmonize with the lead, so the claim never sounds like one person alone. It sits right where late-'60s garage rock, soul, and funk-rock were bleeding into each other.

The lyrics are mostly one phrase, repeated until it turns from statement into chant. In between, they slip in the reasons it needs saying. "Who cares if my hair is a little bit long" waves off a scold. "I'm red and yellow and black and tan, I'm a man!" stretches personhood across every color it can name. And then, tucked in after "doin' my things," comes the tell: "You better believe me." That's not the voice of someone sure of being believed. The pride and the plea sit in the same breath, and the song never settles which one is winning. It just says the word again, louder.

Thunder liked to point out that Bob Dylan, talking to Jann Wenner in Rolling Stone in 1969, named "I'm Alive" among the most powerful records he'd ever heard on the radio. The single still didn't sell enough to keep Thunder's career going. That makes "doin' my thing and singin' my song" land a little harder now. The record insists on a life the market didn't make room for.

By the last run of "I'm alive, I'm alive, I'm alive," it has stopped being information and become breathing, and you end up chanting it along with him, half celebrating and half making sure.
